newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Lebed leaves for rebel Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed leaves for rebel Chechnya.

text.p: Russian security chief Alexander Lebed flew to Chechnya on Thursday for talks with separatist leaders less than a week after signing an ambitious peace deal for the breakaway region.
Interfax news agency, reporting Lebed's departure from Moscow, said he would meet rebel chief-of-staff Aslan Maskhadov, with whom he signed the accord on Saturday, during his two-day mission.
The meeting would take place in the village of Novye Atagi, some 25 km (15 miles) to the south of capital Grozny. A Lebed representative met Maskhadov in the same village on Wednesday.
The meeting is expected to try to iron out problems in implementing the peace deal, which defers a decision on Chechnya's political status for five years.

Lebed is President Boris Yeltsin's representative in Chechnya, but the 65-year-old president, who dropped from sight in late June and is now on holiday near Moscow, has not publicly backed Lebed's peace deal.
Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, seen as a rival to Lebed, has given the accord his guarded approval.
The first test of the deal is expected to be on Friday, the fifth anniversary of Chechnya's self-declared independence.
Interfax said Maskhadov had promised to ban celebratory parades in Grozny and have only religious ceremonies there.

With peace tentatively setting in across the region after nearly 21 months of war and tens of thousands of deaths, Chechnya's ruined capital, Grozny, is setting out on the long road to reconstruction with more hope than confidence.

A group of middle-aged women, hair bundled up in headscarves, bent double sweeping the streets were one of the visible reminders on Wednesday of the huge effort that will be needed rebuild what was once a bustling city of 400,000.

They raised huge clouds of dust as they swept bomb-blasted stone and twisted metal debris into piles. It seemed a near futile effort against the backdrop of buildings blown apart in the fighting, crater-pocked roads and tangles of metal left by anything from tramlines to knocked-out Russian tanks.

"We have cleared up after each ceasefire agreement and we hope that this will be the last time," said Zina Matashev, 51, one of the woman sweeping the roads. "Now we have peace so let them leave us in peace," she added, tears welling in her eyes.
Another signs of a return to something like normality after the rebels seized the city in last month's battle was the market on Ulitsa Mira (Peace Street), where traders worked flat out.
Fery Aalame, head of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) in Grozny, said some 80,000 to 100,000 people may have been forced to flee Grozny by the fighting.
"The civilian population has suffered a lot, there is a complete lack of clean water...there is no medical structure," Aalame told reporters in the capital.
The Red Cross is helping to restart water supplies and was bringing in some 600,000 litres (132,000 gallons) a day to the civilian population. It is also supplying food and medicines.
